The fog rolled in like a gray tide, swallowing the cliffs of Blackwood Point until the world was nothing but damp silence and the rhythmic *thrum* of the lighthouse beam. Elias Thorne, seventy years old and stiff-kneed, wiped the condensation from the lantern room glass. He had kept this light for forty years, a solitary sentinel against the dark, but tonight, the darkness felt heavier, more intentional.

A knock at the heavy oak door of the keeper’s cottage broke the spell. It wasn’t the wind; the wind didn’t knock. It rapped with three precise, deliberate taps.

Elias descended the spiral stairs, his joints protesting each step. He opened the door to find no one standing there, only a single envelope resting on the threshold, sealed with wax the color of dried blood. The paper was thick, cream-colored, and smelled faintly of ozone and old rain.

His hands trembled as he broke the seal. The handwriting inside was jagged, hurried, written in ink that shimmered with an iridescent sheen.

*Elias,*

*If you are reading this, the storm has come early. Do not trust the radio. Do not trust the men in the gray coats who will arrive at dawn. They are not here to save the light; they are here to extinguish it. The light is not just a guide for ships, Elias. It is a anchor for time itself. When the beam flickers, the timeline fractures. You must keep the wick trimmed, the oil full, and the lens clean. No matter what they say, no matter what you see in the water, do not let the light go out.*

*— E.T., 2124*

Elias stared at the signature. His own initials. His own name, written by a hand that did not yet exist. A cold chill, sharper than the sea spray, crawled up his spine. He looked out the window. The fog had thickened, but within it, shapes were moving. Not ships. Figures. Tall, silent silhouettes standing on the rocks below, watching the tower.

He rushed to the lantern room, his heart hammering against his ribs. The great Fresnel lens turned slowly, casting its golden eye across the churning sea.
